newsitem.title: UK: US debt preferred, Italy also gains - Paribas poll.
newsitem.headline: US debt preferred, Italy also gains - Paribas poll.

text.p: Investors have raised their exposure to U.S. Treasuries during the second quarter while in Europe, Italian debt allocations have increased significantly, according to a survey by Paribas Capital Markets on Thursday.
Exposure to global bonds in general has increased in an environment of falling yields.
The survey was undertaken between June 30 and July 8 to reflect the changes made to investor portfolios during the second quarter 1997. In all, 90 multi-currency investors were canvassed.
The allocations were measured in an index from zero to 100, 100 being the maximum overweight.
The largest increases were recorded in U.S. Treasury, Spanish, Italian and Swedish bond markets.
Allocations in Treasuries rose by eight points to the overweight level of 64.

"The combination of softer economic growth, reduced rate hike fear and short durations positions at the end of Q1 combined to force investors to buy dollar bonds during the course of Q2," Paribas said in a statement.
Paribas said there had been a decisive reallocation toward high yield European markets, Italy in particular.
Italian bond allocations were at 51, a gain of 11 points in the quarter, while Swedish bonds were up seven points at 54 and Spanish bonds up four at 46.
Duration of bonds held in portfolio had increased in most markets, but with the exception of the German Bund, Danish bond and British gilt markets, current levels were only neutral or modestly short.
In terms of allocation, gilts were at 68, up three points, whereas Bunds were down four points at 56.
At the other end of the scale, investors have shown no interest in entering the Japanese Government Bond market.

"Total exposure, at 19 is near liquidation levels," Paribas said. "However there has been a sharp increase in the currency position, up 10 to 33, evidence of investors participating in the currency's strong rally during the quarter."

Paribas also conducted a survey to determine investor confidence in the creation of European economic and monetary union (EMU), the timetable for introduction and which countries would join at the start of EMU.
"Of the 80 respondents all, 100 percent...believed EMU will indeed be established," Paribas said.
Most saw EMU starting on schedule in 1999 with only five percent looking for a small delay until 2000 and one percent anticipating a start date in 2001.
A broader EMU was also expected with 93 percent seeing Ireland, and 90 percent seeing Spain, being included in the first stage.
